q: A page needs 12 files, 100 ms each. The browser uses HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections. About how long does it take?
why: Each connection does one request at a time. Six run together, then six more. That is two rounds of 100 ms.

q: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive lets one connection carry two requests at the same moment.
why: No. Keep-alive only reuses the connection for the next request, one after the other. Doing two at once needs HTTP/2 streams.

q: What is head-of-line blocking at the HTTP level in HTTP/1.1?
options: A request waits behind the one in front of it on the same connection
The server runs out of memory
A packet is lost and TCP waits
The browser blocks the first request
why: A connection answers requests in order. A slow first answer holds back all the others on that connection. Browsers open six connections to soften this.

q: Which of these does HTTP/2 add compared with HTTP/1.1?
options: A new transport called QUIC over UDP
why: HTTP/2 has multiplexed streams, HPACK and binary frames, all over TCP. QUIC over UDP belongs to HTTP/3.

q: One packet is lost on an HTTP/2 connection. What happens?
options: Only the stream that owned the packet waits
Every stream on that TCP connection waits
Nothing, HTTP/2 repairs it with no delay
The browser opens six new connections
why: TCP gives data to the app in order, and it does not know about streams. One missing packet holds everything behind it.

q: Put these in order, from the oldest protocol to the newest.
why: HTTP/1.1 came first, then HTTP/2 with multiplexing, then HTTP/3 which moves to QUIC over UDP.

options: UDP is more reliable than TCP
QUIC builds its own reliability and streams on top of UDP, and new TCP changes are hard to roll out
Browsers cannot use TCP any more
why: QUIC runs in user space on UDP. It adds its own loss repair and keeps streams apart. Changing TCP would need every router and system to update.

q: A fresh HTTP/3 connection needs this many round trips before the first request is sent. Type the number.
why: QUIC joins the connection and the TLS 1.3 handshake, so it needs 1 round trip. HTTP/2 with TLS 1.3 needs 2.

q: Why can a server not accept every request sent in 0-RTT?
options: An attacker can copy and replay the first packet
why: 0-RTT data has no replay protection. So servers allow it for safe requests such as GET, and refuse POST.

q: A phone moves from Wi-Fi to mobile data. An HTTP/3 connection can keep going, because QUIC names a connection by an ID and not by IP addresses.
why: This is connection migration. A TCP connection is named by the four address numbers, so HTTP/2 must open a new connection.

q: How does the browser learn that a site also speaks HTTP/3?
why: A header like alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 says h3 is on port 443 for a day. The next visit can try QUIC.

q: Which sits inside the TLS hello and lets the client and server pick h2 or http/1.1?
why: ALPN is a TLS extension. The client lists what it speaks and the server picks one.

q: Your site now speaks HTTP/3. What must you do on the server side?
options: Send an Alt-Svc header on the TCP answers
Keep HTTP/2 on as the fallback
why: Open UDP 443, advertise with Alt-Svc, and keep TCP and HTTP/2 because some networks block UDP.

q: A response has Cache-Control: no-cache. What does it mean?
options: Do not store it at all
The cache may keep it but must ask the server before reusing it
It stays fresh for a year
It is always served from the CDN
why: no-cache means revalidate before reuse, usually with an ETag and a 304. no-store is the one that forbids keeping it.
